title: HttpClient and just enough RxJS
goal: Fetch data in Angular with HttpClient and understand Observables well enough to use them confidently.

concepts: provideHttpClient(withFetch()) in app.config.ts
HttpClient.get<T>(url) returns an Observable (lazy: nothing happens until subscribed)
Observable vs Promise: many values, cancellable, lazy
pipe with map, catchError, tap; switchMap for 'latest request wins'
Turning Observables into signals with toSignal, or into promises with firstValueFrom
Put HTTP calls in services, not components

build.task: In angular-playground, create UsersApi (service) using HttpClient against https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com: getUsers(), getUser(id), getUserPosts(id), with typed interfaces. Build /users (list, using toSignal) and /users/:id (detail with the user's posts). Then build a live search box using a FormControl's valueChanges with debounceTime(300), distinctUntilChanged() and switchMap to call https://api.github.com/search/users?q=… and show results. Write docs/rxjs.md explaining each operator you used in your own words.
acceptance: provideHttpClient(withFetch()) configured
All HTTP calls live in services with typed return values
Users list and detail pages work, including direct URL loads
Search uses debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged and switchMap (check the Network tab: old requests are cancelled)
docs/rxjs.md explains each operator in your own words

hints: users = toSignal(this.api.getUsers(), { initialValue: [] }); then @for (u of users(); track u.id) in the template.
results = toSignal(this.search.valueChanges.pipe(debounceTime(300), distinctUntilChanged(), switchMap(q => q ? this.api.searchGithub(q) : of([]))), { initialValue: [] }).
switchMap unsubscribes from the previous inner request when a new value arrives. HttpClient then cancels that request, and you'll see it marked as cancelled in DevTools.
proof: Commit with the services, pages and docs/rxjs.md.

explainBack.q: Why doesn't this.http.get(url) send a request until something subscribes?
lookFor: each subscription sends a new request

explainBack.q: Explain what switchMap does in your search and what bug it prevents.
lookFor: maps each query to a request
prevents stale results arriving out of order

lastHintExplanation: Observables are lazy: http.get only describes a request, and each subscription (via subscribe, toSignal or firstValueFrom) actually sends one. In the search pipe, debounceTime waits for a typing pause, distinctUntilChanged skips repeated queries, and switchMap starts a request per query while cancelling the previous one, so a slow old response can't overwrite newer results.

predict.q: const obs = this.http.get('/api/x'); obs.subscribe(); obs.subscribe(); How many HTTP requests are sent?
predict.why: Each subscription to a cold HTTP observable sends its own request.

title: Full CRUD with a mock REST API
goal: Create, read, update and delete data on a REST API from Angular, keeping the UI in sync.

concepts: json-server: a fake REST API from a db.json file
HTTP verbs in HttpClient: get, post, put, patch, delete
Environment config for the API base URL
Updating local state after server responses (or optimistic updates with rollback)
Error handling with catchError and user-friendly messages
HTTP status codes you'll see: 200, 201, 204, 400, 404, 500

build.task: Move your angular-notes app from localStorage to a REST API. Add api/db.json with a notes array and run npx json-server api/db.json --port 3001. Create NotesApi (service) with list, get, create (POST), update (PATCH), remove (DELETE), with the base URL from an environment file. NotesStore now loads from the API and updates its signals from server responses. Show a loading skeleton while listing, disable buttons while saving, and show error toasts if the server is down (stop json-server to test). Add an npm script "api" to start json-server.

starterFiles.name: api/db.json

acceptance: All CRUD operations hit the API (visible in the Network tab and in db.json)
Base URL comes from environment config, not hard-coded in services
Loading skeleton on list; save/delete buttons disabled while in flight
With the API stopped, the app shows friendly errors and doesn't break
npm run api starts the mock server; README updated with run steps

hints: create(note: NewNote) { return this.http.post<Note>(`${this.base}/notes`, note); } The server returns the saved note including its id.

In the store: this.saving.set(true); try { const saved = await firstValueFrom(this.api.create(n)); this._notes.update(list => [saved, ...list]); } catch { toast.error(...) } finally { this.saving.set(false); }
Run both servers in two terminals: npm run api and ng serve. If you get CORS errors, check the URL and port; json-server allows CORS by default.
proof: Commit with the API service, updated store and db.json.

explainBack.q: When you create a note, why do you add the server's response to the list instead of the form value?
lookFor: response may differ from what was sent

explainBack.q: PUT vs PATCH: which did you use for updates and why?

lastHintExplanation: The server decides the final record: it assigns the id and timestamps and may normalise fields, so adding its response keeps your state honest. PUT replaces the whole resource with what you send; PATCH updates only the fields you send, which is safer when you edit just a title or a pinned flag.

title: Interceptors, loading state and retries
goal: Handle cross-cutting HTTP concerns (base URL, headers, errors, loading) once, with interceptors.

concepts: Functional interceptors: HttpInterceptorFn and withInterceptors([...])
Cloning requests to add headers (Authorization comes in Phase 4)
A global error interceptor that shows toasts for 5xx and network errors
A loading interceptor with a pending-requests counter signal
retry({ count, delay }) for flaky GET requests only
Why not to retry POST blindly (duplicate creates)

build.task: In angular-notes, add three functional interceptors: (1) apiPrefixInterceptor: requests starting with /api get the environment base URL; (2) loadingInterceptor: increments a LoadingService pending signal and decrements it in finalize; show a thin progress bar at the top of the app while pending() > 0; (3) errorInterceptor: maps network errors and 5xx to a friendly toast, and 404 to a 'not found' message, then rethrows. Add retry with 2 attempts and a 500 ms delay to GET requests only. Remove duplicated try/catch toasts from components.
acceptance: Three interceptors registered with withInterceptors in the right order
Services use relative /api/... URLs
Top progress bar shows during any request
Friendly toasts for network/5xx errors without per-component code
GETs retry twice with a delay; POST/PATCH/DELETE never retry

hints: export const loadingInterceptor: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) => { const l = inject(LoadingService); l.start(); return next(req).pipe(finalize(() => l.stop())); };
Prefix: if (req.url.startsWith('/api')) req = req.clone({ url: environment.apiUrl + req.url.slice(4) });
Retry only GETs: next(req).pipe(req.method === 'GET' ? retry({ count: 2, delay: 500 }) : identity). Test by stopping json-server and watching the Network tab.

explainBack.q: Why use interceptors instead of handling errors and loading in every component?
Why shouldn't you automatically retry POST requests?
lookFor: could create duplicates if the first actually succeeded

lastHintExplanation: Interceptors wrap every request, so things every call needs (base URL, headers, loading count, error toasts) live in one place instead of being copied into each component. GET is safe to repeat; POST isn't idempotent. If a POST succeeded but its response was lost, retrying would create a duplicate record.

predict.q: An interceptor does req.headers.set('X-App', '1') and then next(req). Does the header get sent?
options: No, requests are immutable; you must clone
predict.why: HttpRequest is immutable; set() returns new headers. Use req.clone({ setHeaders: ... }).

title: Project: book finder (part 1)
goal: Build a polished Angular app on a real public API: search, results, pagination and good UX states.

concepts: Reading a real API's docs and response shape (Open Library)
Mapping API responses to your own clean interfaces
Search state in the URL (query params) for shareable links
Pagination with page and limit
Image fallbacks for missing covers

build.task: Create a NEW repo book-finder (Angular + Tailwind). Search page: a search box synced to ?q=&page=, debounced; results grid showing cover, title, authors and first-publish year; pagination (20 per page) with Previous/Next and 'Page X of Y'; skeleton cards while loading; empty and error states; a fallback image when there's no cover. Map Open Library's response to your own Book interface in a BooksApi service (components never see the raw API shape).
acceptance: Search is debounced and reflected in the URL; reloading keeps the results
Pagination works and shows the total pages
Raw API types are mapped to a clean Book interface in the service
Skeleton, empty and error states all reachable
Missing covers show a fallback; images have alt text and lazy loading

hints: Search: https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=harry+potter&page=1&limit=20&fields=key,title,author_name,first_publish_year,cover_i. The fields parameter makes responses much smaller.
Cover URL: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/{cover_i}-M.jpg. If cover_i is missing, use a local placeholder in public/.
Total pages: Math.ceil(numFound / 20). Drive everything from route query params: q = input(''), page = input(1, { transform: numberAttribute }).

explainBack.q: Why map the API response to your own Book interface?
lookFor: components don't depend on the API's shape
one place to change if the API changes

explainBack.q: How does putting q and page in the URL improve the app?

lastHintExplanation: Mapping raw responses into your own Book interface means only BooksApi knows Open Library's field names (author_name, cover_i). If the API changes, you fix one file. Keeping q and page in the URL makes the URL the state: links can be shared, reloads restore the results, and the browser's back button walks through earlier searches.

title: Project: book finder (part 2) and deploy
goal: Add details and favourites to the book finder, then deploy it.

concepts: Combining requests with forkJoin (work + author details)
Favourites in a signal store persisted to localStorage
Route-level loading with resolvers or component loading state
Building for production: ng build, base href
Deploying an Angular app to GitHub Pages (angular-cli-ghpages) or Netlify

build.task: Add /books/:workId: fetch the work (https://openlibrary.org/works/{id}.json) and its first author in parallel, and show cover, description (handle string or { value } shapes), subjects (first 10 as chips) and author name. Add a favourites store (signals + localStorage) with a heart toggle on cards and the detail page, plus a /favourites page. Deploy to GitHub Pages (ng build --base-href /book-finder/ then npx angular-cli-ghpages --dir=dist/book-finder/browser) and add a 404.html copy of index.html so deep links work. Update the README with a screenshot and live link.
acceptance: Detail page loads work and author in parallel (forkJoin), handling both description shapes
Favourites toggle on cards and detail; /favourites lists them; persisted
Deployed and working at the live URL, including reloading a deep link like /book-finder/books/OL82563W
README has a screenshot, live link, features and tech
Lighthouse Performance and Accessibility 90+ on the search page

hints: description can be a string or an object: typeof d === 'string' ? d : d?.value ?? 'No description'.
forkJoin({ work: this.getWork(id), author: this.getAuthor(authorKey) }) emits once when both complete. Get the author key from work.authors[0].author.key.
GitHub Pages has no server-side routing, so reloading /book-finder/books/x returns 404. Copying index.html to 404.html makes the Angular app load and route correctly.
proof: Live URL of your deployed book finder.

explainBack.q: Why did deep-link reloads 404 on GitHub Pages, and how did 404.html fix it?
lookFor: static host looks for a real file at that path
Angular routes exist only in the browser
404.html serves the app which then routes

explainBack.q: What does forkJoin do and when would it be the wrong choice?
lookFor: runs observables in parallel, emits when all complete
wrong if one never completes or for streams
fails if any errors unless handled

lastHintExplanation: Angular routes exist only in the browser. GitHub Pages is a static file host, so reloading /books/x makes it look for a real file and return 404. Serving index.html as 404.html loads the app, and Angular's router then shows the right page. forkJoin waits for all inner observables to complete and emits their last values together, so it suits one-shot HTTP calls, not endless streams.

predict.q: forkJoin([http.get(a), http.get(b)]) and request b fails. What happens?
predict.why: forkJoin errors if any inner observable errors (unless you catchError inside).

title: Phase 3 review: Angular machine coding
goal: Prove Phase 3 stuck by building a small Angular feature from scratch, timed, then plan your weak spots.

concepts: Phase 3 summary: TypeScript, Tailwind, components, signals, services, routing, forms, HTTP
Machine-coding rounds: plan for 5 minutes, build the core first, polish last
Honest self-assessment

build.task: Timed (2 hours, no notes for the first 75 minutes): new Angular app 'contact-manager' with Tailwind. Use json-server for /contacts. Features: list with search (debounced) and sort; add/edit form (reactive, validated: name required, email valid, phone Indian mobile); delete with confirmation; a detail route; loading and error states via an interceptor. Commit 'checkpoint: no notes' at 75 minutes. Then write docs/phase3-review.md: what you built unaided, what you looked up, your top 3 weak topics, and a plan for them.
acceptance: 'checkpoint: no notes' commit within 75 minutes
List, search, sort, add, edit, delete and detail all work against json-server
Validated reactive form with clear messages
Loading/error handled through an interceptor
phase3-review.md is honest and specific

hints: Spend the first 5–10 minutes writing the routes, the Contact interface and the service method names. Then build list → form → detail → polish.
If something blocks you for more than 10 minutes in the no-notes part, leave a TODO and move on.
Reuse patterns, not files: you already wrote all of these pieces in the last 4 weeks.
proof: Links to the checkpoint commit and the final commit.

explainBack.q: Which part of the build was slowest, and why?
lookFor: honest cause (forgot API, typing issues, etc.)

explainBack.q: Explain your app's data flow from the API to the list on screen.

lastHintExplanation: In a machine-coding round, interviewers look for a working core first: clear data flow (service → state → components), validation, and handled loading and error states. Then they look for polish. Planning the model and routes before coding saves time and stops you painting yourself into a corner.
